title: Final Words from Prison
subtitle: Selected passages from 2 Timothy and Philippians
source: Verses drawn from the King James Version (1611, public domain). Editorial framing by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: Learning to be content
paragraphs: Writing to the Philippians from his first Roman imprisonment, Paul thanks the church for the gift Epaphroditus has brought him, and uses the occasion to teach them what he has learned in chains.

He says he has learned, in whatsoever state he finds himself, to be content. He knows how to be abased, and he knows how to abound; everywhere, and in all things, he is instructed both to be full and to be hungry. The famous summary verse follows: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

Paul does not say he was born this way. He says he learned it. The chains, the cold, the daily uncertainty of whether tomorrow will bring a sword or a meal, have schooled him in a kind of freedom he could not have known on the road.
notes: The Greek 'autarkes', here rendered 'content', is the same word the Stoics used for self-sufficiency. Paul subverts it. The Christian autarky is not independence but utter dependence on Christ, which leaves nothing in the world able to take a man's peace.
Philippians was written from Rome around 62, during the imprisonment Acts ends with. The Philippian church had supported Paul materially from the beginning of his work in Macedonia.

sections.title: I have finished my course
paragraphs: Years later, in chains again and this time awaiting the sword, Paul writes his second letter to Timothy from a Roman prison cell. It is the last surviving letter from his hand. He tells Timothy to come quickly, to bring his cloak from Troas, and to bring the books, especially the parchments.

Then he reaches the verses the Orthodox Church reads at his feast and at every memorial of an apostle. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love His appearing.

The crown Paul speaks of is the Greek athletic prize, the wreath the runner receives at the end of the race. He does not say he has won; he says he has finished. The Christian race is run to the end. The reward is the appearing of Christ, the day for which the apostle has now been waiting forty years.
notes: Second Timothy was written from Rome around 67, during Paul's second and final imprisonment under Nero. He was beheaded on the Ostian Way some time after.
'All them also that love His appearing' is Paul's reminder that the apostolic crown is not reserved for apostles. Every Christian who longs for Christ's return runs the same race for the same prize.
